hero.name: Suresh
hero.who: a 44-year-old pharmacist in Coimbatore who wants to invest but fears hype and panic

story.h: The tip in the chemists' group
story.b: Suresh runs a medical shop near Gandhipuram in Coimbatore. For twenty years he has saved in fixed deposits, and his money feels like it is standing still. The chemists' WhatsApp group is full of share tips. Last year a distributor swore a small company would double, so Suresh bought. It fell sharply, and he sold in a panic at eleven one night. The loss still sits in his trading app. Now his daughter is in Class 9, college fees are coming, and he wants to invest properly. But every time he opens the app, it feels like gambling. Tonight another message arrives in the group. Buy before Monday, it says, or regret it.

ask.q: Another hot tip arrives in the group. What is the wisest thing for Suresh to do first?
o: Buy a small amount before Monday, just in case it is right
Pause and learn the difference between investing and betting on tips
Give up on shares forever and keep everything in fixed deposits
ask.why: Buying on a rumour, even a small amount, repeats last year's mistake. Giving up shares forever ignores that sensible, patient investing can serve long goals like college fees. Learning what real investing means gives him a way to act without gambling.

chapters.take: Before you put money in, know whether you are investing or betting.

story.b: One quiet afternoon, between customers, Suresh lists everything he owns on the back of a prescription notepad. The fixed deposits. His PPF account. The small company from the tip. Two shares he bought because a TV anchor sounded confident. Next to each, he asks three honest questions. Did he study the business? Is his money reasonably safe? Is he expecting a sensible return, or a miracle? Most of his shares get the label speculation. That does not make him a fool, he realises. It just means he was betting while calling it investing. He decides that any betting money will now be small, separate and clearly named, and everything else will be studied first.

ask.q: Suresh still wants a little money for risky bets. What is the sensible way to do it?
o: Keep a small, separate amount, clearly labelled as speculation
Mix it into his main savings so any gains help the family
Call the bets long-term investments so his wife will not worry
ask.why: Speculating knowingly, with a small sum he can afford to lose, is his choice to make. The danger is confusion. Mixing bets into family savings or renaming them as investments hides the risk, and that is how real money gets hurt.

chapters.take: Betting is not investing. Never let the two get mixed up.

story.b: A few months later, markets drop sharply on some world news. The chemists' group explodes. Sell everything, one message says. Another posts a red chart covered in crying faces. Suresh feels his stomach tighten. Then he thinks of his own shop. Last monsoon, a rumour spread that a common fever medicine would run short. People queued and paid double. A month later the shelves were full and the price was normal again. The medicine had not changed at all, only the mood. So Suresh asks a calmer question about the companies he owns. Has the business itself changed, or just the crowd's feelings? He reads the news properly, finds nothing broken, and does not sell.

ask.q: Prices fall sharply and the group shouts to sell everything. What should Suresh check first?
o: How much the price has fallen since the day he bought
What most of the people in the group are doing
Whether the business itself has changed, or only the mood
ask.why: The size of the fall and the crowd's panic both reflect feelings, not facts about the business. If the business is still sound, the price drop is just mood, and he is free to ignore it. Checking the business first stops him from selling in fear.

chapters.take: Prices swing with moods. Ask whether the business has really changed.

story.b: Suresh starts studying one company he understands well, a maker of medical supplies whose products pass through his shop every week. He reads its yearly reports slowly, over many evenings, and works out a rough idea of what the business might be worth. Today's price is close to his estimate. The old Suresh would have bought at once. Now he asks a harder question. What if his estimate is wrong? He is a pharmacist, not an analyst, and he will make mistakes. So he decides to buy only if the price falls well below his estimate, leaving a cushion for errors. He writes his number on a card and waits.

ask.q: The company Suresh studied trades close to what he thinks it is worth. What should he do?
o: Wait for a price well below his estimate, leaving room for his mistakes
Buy now, since his estimate is careful and probably right
Buy double, because a business he understands is safe at any price
ask.why: Even careful estimates can be wrong. Buying near full value leaves no cushion if he has misjudged, and no business is safe at any price. Waiting for a price well below his estimate builds in room for error, which protects him when mistakes happen.

chapters.take: Leave room for being wrong, because sometimes you will be.

story.b: Suresh tries reading company reports after closing the shop at ten, and keeps falling asleep over them. One Sunday he counts his hours honestly. The shop runs six and a half days a week. He has about two hours to spare for investing, and he wants those hours to be calm. That settles it. He is not a bargain hunter, and pretending to be one would only lead to sloppy choices. So he keeps an emergency fund in fixed deposits, starts a monthly SIP in a low-cost, diversified index fund for his daughter's college, and keeps only a small part for the rare company he truly understands. His friend Ganesh, a retired teacher, loves deep research. That suits Ganesh.

ask.q: Suresh has about two hours a week for investing. Which approach suits him best?
o: Hunt for bargain shares late at night after closing the shop
Follow the group's tips, since others are doing the research
Keep a simple, diversified plan, like a monthly SIP in an index fund
ask.why: Hunting bargains needs steady, serious research time, and midnight reading after a long shift is not that. Tips just borrow other people's guesses. With little time, a simple diversified plan matches his effort to his expectations, which is the whole point of knowing his type.

chapters.take: Match your investing style to the time and effort you can truly give.

story.b: Six months in, two tests arrive close together. First, a new share listing becomes the talk of the town, and a neighbour boasts of quick profits. Suresh feels a greedy itch to jump in. A few weeks later, markets fall again and his SIP shows a loss. Now he feels the opposite itch, to stop everything until things look safe. He notices that both feelings are loud, and both come from the crowd, not his plan. So on a calm Sunday he writes three rules on a small card and keeps it in his wallet. I do not stop my SIP when prices fall. I do not buy because the group is excited. I review once a year, in April.

ask.q: His SIP shows a loss and Suresh wants to stop it until markets look better. What should he do?
o: Stop the SIP now and restart once prices look safe again
Follow his written rule and keep the SIP going as planned
Move everything into the fund that rose most last month
ask.why: Stopping when prices fall and chasing last month's winner are both driven by feeling, not by plan, and they can do more damage than a weak market. A rule written on a calm day protects him from his own panic and greed.

chapters.take: Your own panic and greed are the biggest risks. Write rules on calm days.

story.b: A year later, the chemists' group still buzzes with tips, and Suresh reads them the way he reads the weather forecast. Interesting, but not an instruction. His SIP runs quietly each month. The emergency fund sits in its FD. A chart on his cupboard tracks his daughter's college goal, slowly filling. When the medical supplies company fell well below his estimate one month, he bought a small amount, as planned, and labelled it clearly. Last month the market dipped again. Suresh looked at the card in his wallet, put it back and went on counting strips of tablets. His wife asked if he was worried. He said he had a plan, and slept well.

chapters.take: A calm plan protects your money better than any clever tip.
